Part 0 · IntroductionNext: Summary

Why do we even care?

Text Diffusion (TD) is one of the popular alternatives to traditional Autoregressive (AR) decoding when it comes to generative AI. The field mostly develops around the promise that one can design better algorithms more suited to the hardware at hand, making heavy use of parallel compute. It is fair to say that diffusion Language Models (dLMs), the models that TD decodes, are still mostly in their infancy and that many research questions are still open. We broadly classify them into two categories:

  • Capabilities: Can dLMs deliver intelligent models on par with (or better than) their AR counterparts? Improving the capabilities of native dLMs is an active field of research. It is still unclear which diffusion model approach and representation will yield the best results: continuous/discrete modeling, vocabulary embedding or one-hot token representation, etc.
  • Serving speed: How much faster can a dLM be compared with AR? This discussion is the topic of this blogpost. We will see that it requires a good understanding of rooflines, hardware specifications but also kernel engineering and serving software.

Therefore, in the rest of this blogpost, we do not concern ourselves with discussion on the quality of dLMs. Our only goal is to identify in which scenarios, both in theory and in practice, dLMs can provide substantial serving gains over AR.

Who is this blogpost for?

The aim of this blogpost is entirely pedagogical. I do not claim any significant theoretical or practical novelty. The blogpost is intended for researchers and engineers who are curious about the differences between TD and AR when it comes to serving. I am not an expert on these topics myself, and I hope that this blogpost serves as a gentle introduction for the curious reader.

Our mental model

An AR model generates one token per forward pass1. On the other hand, in the TD paradigm, a canvas of \(b\) tokens is generated in \(S\) forward passes. In addition, TD runs one last forward pass over the finished canvas, with a causal mask, in order to write its keys and values to the KV cache for the next canvas: the commit pass. Hence, a key quantity that will arise in all of our theoretical considerations is the ratio \(\frac{b}{S + 1}\) (in the case where a denoising pass costs as much as the commit pass). This ratio is called the Tokens per Forward Pass (or TPF) and will guide our reasoning throughout the blogpost. An illustration of the AR and TD paradigms is given in Figure 1. Our approach closely follows the one of DiffusionGemma.

Figure 1

In the same 15 passes, AR commits 15 tokens and TD commits a canvas of 256.

A canvas of \(b = 256\) positions, \(S = 14\) denoising passes and one commit pass, so \(15\) passes per canvas and \(\mathrm{TPF} = b/(S+1) = 17.1\) tokens per forward pass.

A full generation with TD is shown in Figure 2 below, and explained in Section 3 of the technical report. We highlight that the KV cache commit uses a causal encoder (a causal mask), while the parallel generation uses a diffusion decoder. In DiffusionGemma the two networks share their parameters; therefore, denoting \(r\) the cost of a denoising pass relative to the commit pass, we have \(r = 1\), but other choices are of course possible. Block diffusion with encoder-decoder architectures is common in the literature, see Encoder-Decoder Diffusion Language Models for Efficient Training and Inference for instance.

Figure 2

The causal encoder writes the KV cache; the bidirectional decoder only reads it.

An illustration of the inference in DiffusionGemma. The noise level \(t\) goes from 1 to 0 over the \(S\) denoising passes, in steps of \(\Delta t = 1/S\), and \(x_0\) is the clean canvas. We briefly highlight the dependency of each step on the self-conditioning signal \(s_t\). We will discuss the role of self-conditioning in more detail when deriving rooflines.

Rooflines and gains

The main object of interest in this blogpost is the throughput. The ratio of the TD throughput and the AR throughput, for the same model on the same accelerator and at the same batch size \(B\) and context \(C\) (i.e., tokens which are already in the KV cache), will be called the gain and denoted \(\Gamma\). There are many other notions of "speed" that could be considered, like end-to-end latency and Time To First Token (TTFT). For simplicity, we will not investigate TTFT and the other (important!) aspects of serving. We will mostly consider gains over a grid of batch sizes \(B\) and contexts \(C\). Different batch sizes and contexts correspond to different workloads:

  • For instance, a high batch size is associated with cloud serving most of the time (Kwon et al., 2023; Pope et al., 2022).
  • Long context can appear in many situations but is very common in multi-turn and highly agentic scenarios (Gao et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026).

Of course, hardware specifications also enter the picture to determine which paradigm yields the best throughput. We will take all of these factors into consideration and try to predict as precisely as possible the value of the gain \(\Gamma\) and discuss when \(\Gamma > 1\), i.e., when TD is beneficial.

This analysis will be guided by previous works on the roofline model (Williams et al., 2009). While this blogpost is mostly self-contained, we warmly recommend the following excellent references: Pope et al. (2022) and Austin et al. (2025).

From theory to practice

Theoretical inference results are only useful if they inform the practitioner. While the bounds of Parts 1–4 seem fairly robust at first sight, they rely on three assumptions that are often violated in practice:

  • Hardware ceilings: First, hardware ceilings differ from what is announced on the datasheet. In Part 5, we measure those empirical ceilings on our chosen hardware (H200).
  • Expert routing: Second, the number of distinct experts that a forward pass touches is extremely important to derive proper inference gains. In the theoretical results, we take our best shot at approximating it using an independence assumption (A3): the tokens of a pass choose their experts independently and uniformly. In practice, a pass touches fewer experts than this assumption predicts, which raises the bound at small batch and lowers it at large batch. In Part 5, we measure the experts touched per Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer and per forward pass for the given workload.
  • Kernel engineering: Finally, while the first two points correspond to limitations of the datasheet and the theoretical roofline work, we also need to face the harsh truth that kernels do not run at their rooflines. While we can acknowledge some inefficiencies, TD still requires some kernel engineering work in the case of DiffusionGemma in order to run as efficiently as its AR counterpart. Part 6 describes how every kernel is measured and fixes defects of the serving engine, Part 7 rewrites the two kernels that lag furthest behind their rooflines, and Part 8 compares the measured gain with the bound (Figure 3).

(a) is the roofline bound of the exact accounting with datasheet rates and independent routing (A3); (b) uses the ceilings measured on this H200; (c) also uses the expert counts measured in the same runs; (d), in magenta, is the gain measured in vLLM. All the practical chapters, Parts 5–8, are evaluated under a common setting.

  • Models: DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B (TD) and Gemma 4 26B-A4B (AR), which has the same backbone.
  • Accelerator: one H200 SXM.
  • Engine: vLLM 0.28.0 with CUDA graphs (methodology and fixes are described in Part 6); FP8 weights (8-bit floats), BF16 KV cache (16-bit floats).
  • Workload (details in Part 6):
    • Prompts: passages cut from the PG-19 test books, each followed by a request for a long essay about the passage, in the model's chat template.
    • Grid: \(B \in \{1, 2, 4, \dots, 64\}\) and prompts of \(C \in \{1\text{k}, 4\text{k}, 16\text{k}, 64\text{k}\}\) tokens; 16k is measured up to batch 32 and 64k up to batch 16, 25 points in all.
    • Canvas and passes: \(b = 256\) positions and \(S = 14\) denoising passes2.
    • Sampling: AR at temperature 1, TD with DiffusionGemma's own schedule, from 0.8 at the first denoising pass to 0.43 at the last, using the documented temperature annealing strategy.
  • Code: In addition to this blogpost, we will publish a harness for inference analysis, roofscope (not yet public), which runs the engine, records every kernel and routing decision, and computes the rooflines.

How the blogpost is organised

The blogpost is divided into two halves, mapped in Figure 4:

  • In Parts 1–4, we provide a theoretical model of TD and AR rooflines and give a simple formula for the gain \(\Gamma\). We discuss different scenarios depending on hardware and workload.
  • In Parts 5–8, we measure \(\Gamma\) for DiffusionGemma on one H200 on PG-19, a long-context language modeling benchmark (see the repository). We fix several issues in the serving of TD (engine fixes in Part 6, kernel engineering in Part 7) in order to obtain comparable efficiencies between AR and TD. Finally, we compare our measured throughput with the theoretical bounds of Parts 1–4 and provide some recommendations for evaluating the inference of TD.

A few notable chapters can be read standalone:

  • Part 3 contains the exact maps over batch and context, and a calculator for any accelerator and model.
  • Part 4 is a set of exercises, with folded solutions, to assess the performance of TD over AR for different hardware and workloads.

We made a few (arbitrary) choices to help the reader throughout the blogpost:

  • Colours: AR quantities are blue, TD quantities orange and measured quantities magenta, in the equations and in the figures.
  • Symbols: a click on a formula lists the symbols it uses, and the Symbols page lists them all.

Acknowledgments

I would like to thank Alexandre Galashov, Patrick Pynadath, Justin Deschenaux, Yazid Janati, Rishi Iyer and Ivan Lobov for their feedback. Rishi Iyer's arithmetic intensity primer for language diffusion derives, for grouped-query attention and MoE layers, the \(b\)-fold gain in intensity that a block of \(b\) queries brings; Parts 1 and 2 refine it with the expert and attention penalties.

Notes

  1. While parallel generation is now also common in AR models through Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and Speculative Sampling (SS), we do not consider those scenarios in the rest of the blogpost. The Conclusion relates TD to speculative decoding among related work. ↩
  2. \(S\) is fixed: every canvas runs all 14 denoising passes and commits all its positions together. DiffusionGemma's own sampler is entropy-bounded with adaptive stopping, and averages about 12 denoising steps and 20 tokens per forward pass (technical report, Table 2). For simplicity, we do not consider such confidence or entropy based samplers, which can considerably improve the throughput of TD; we leave a similar study for future work. ↩
